title: One jersey, one cart line: personalised shirts with a Cart Transform Function
summary: A personalised hockey jersey is really four products: the shirt, the name, the number and the badges. Here is how I made them check out as one line for EV Zug without touching the price.
body: When a fan personalises an EV Zug jersey, the store has to sell four things: the shirt itself, the name on the back, the number and any badges. Behind the scenes each of them is a separate product with its own price, and fulfilment needs to see every one.

The fan sees none of that. They bought one jersey. A cart with four lines, three of which look like add-ons, reads like a mistake, and it gets worse in checkout, where every line repeats with its own image and price.
Merging lines without losing them

Shopify's answer is a Cart Transform Function: a small program that runs inside Shopify's cart and can merge several lines into one bundle line. I wrote it in TypeScript, compiled to WebAssembly, so it runs inside Shopify on every cart change.
What the function returns is short. For every personalised jersey it asks Shopify to merge the lines that belong together under one parent product:

{ "operations": [ { "merge": {
  "cartLines": [ shirt, name, number, badge ],
  "parentVariantId": "gid://shopify/ProductVariant/…",
  "title": "Home jersey, personalised"
} } ] }
Simplified. The real function also has to decide which lines belong to which jersey when a fan buys two.

Two rules mattered more than the code. The total never changes: the bundle costs exactly what its parts cost. And every component stays attached to the order, so fulfilment still sees the name, the number and the badges as separate items to produce.
The parts around it

A bundle line is only as good as the jersey preview that sells it. On the product page I centre the number optically, measuring the rendered glyphs on a canvas and recalculating once the club's webfont has loaded, because a 1 and an 8 that are mathematically centred do not look centred.

The function has its own admin page in the store's companion app, and the same store also runs the live auction page and the German and English order emails. In total, 325 of the store's 907 commits are mine.
The result is the kind of feature nobody notices, which is the point: a fan personalises a shirt, sees one jersey in the cart and pays for one jersey.

title: Moving a store's whole history without sending a single email
summary: Importing tens of thousands of past customers and orders into a live Shopify store would normally email every one of them. Here is how I built a migration app where that cannot happen.
body: When a brand moves from PrestaShop to Shopify, its customer history has to come along: accounts, addresses and years of past orders. Shopify can import all of it through the Admin GraphQL API. By default, it will also politely email every customer an account invitation and a receipt for an order they placed three years ago.
For a store with tens of thousands of customers, that is not a bug report. It is a crisis. So the one hard requirement for this migration app was silence.
Making the mistake impossible, not unlikely

A checkbox or a careful developer is not a guarantee. I wanted the code itself to make sending mail impossible, so the app has exactly one place that creates orders, and the receipt options there are hardcoded:

// The only code path that creates orders (simplified)
const options = {
  sendReceipt: false,
  sendFulfillmentReceipt: false,
  inventoryBehaviour: "BYPASS",
};

Customers are created without a password or an invited state, so Shopify has no reason to send an invitation. And a guard test fails the build if any of the invite mutations is ever referenced anywhere in the code. If someone adds one in a year, the release stops before it reaches a store.
Dry run first, always
The merchant uploads three PrestaShop exports. Nothing is written yet: the app first shows what it parsed, previews of every file, customers it could not match, missing SKUs and rows it will skip.

Only then can they start the import, behind a confirmation that repeats the no-email promise and the exact shop domain it will write to. Customers go in first, then orders from oldest to newest, with live progress and a cancel button. Every run can be repeated safely and ends with a CSV report of every source row.
Built once, used twice
The app ran for the Swiss store and then for the UAE store. Behind it are 17 test suites, and 53 of its 56 commits are mine. The number I am proudest of is the one nobody sees: zero customer emails.

title: From 16.2 MB to 4.5 MB: slimming down a Shopify product page
summary: A colour-variant product page on the new Curaprox store weighed 16.2 MB. Three unglamorous fixes brought it to 4.5 MB before launch. No framework changes, no new apps.
body: Before the new Swiss and UAE Curaprox stores went live, I went through the product pages with Lighthouse and a real Chrome. One colour-variant product page weighed 16.2 MB on mobile. A toothbrush that comes in 36 colours is a nice problem for a brand and a heavy one for a page.
None of the fixes were clever. All of them were about sending less.
1. Images the size they are shown
The gallery was loading images far larger than the space they filled on a phone. Serving properly sized images took the gallery from 13.0 MB to 1.4 MB, on its own the biggest single win.
2. One swatch, drawn once

Each of the 36 colour swatches had the same SVG shape pasted inline. Thirty-six copies of identical markup is invisible to a shopper and very visible in the HTML, so I defined the shape once and referenced it everywhere:

<svg hidden><symbol id="swatch" viewBox="0 0 24 24">…</symbol></svg>

<!-- each of the 36 swatches -->
<svg><use href="#swatch"/></svg>
Simplified. Each swatch still gets its own colour.
The HTML of that 36-colour page went from 2.03 MB to 0.76 MB.
3. Nothing that jumps

On mobile product pages, content shifted after loading in about half of the test runs, with a layout shift score of 0.108. After my fix it was zero in every run. On a slow 3G connection, the bestseller slider now shows all its images after 20.8 seconds instead of 31.7, 34% sooner.
The part that is not about speed

While I was in there, I checked the delivery promises on the UAE product pages against what checkout actually offers. All 84 test cases now match, because a fast page that promises the wrong delivery date is still a bad page.

Measured in my pull requests on unpublished test themes against the live theme, August and September 2026: mobile Lighthouse for page weight, Slow 3G with a cold cache for the slider, repeated runs for layout shift.
